name: Umar Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and you won't be named. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in by eight at the health centre on Canal Street, and the first hour is blood results and hospital letters before the doors open. Then it's fifteen-minute slots until one, the phone list over lunch, and afternoon surgery until half six. A lot of my patients have three or four things going on at once: diabetes, a bad back, a damp flat and a benefits form they need help with. I type my own notes, always have.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is the people who keep coming back, like an old man with heart failure who brings me tomatoes from his allotment every August. Grace, our practice nurse, and I eat lunch in the treatment room most days and swap stories about him. What wears me out is the gap between what people need and what fifteen minutes allows. Most evenings I sit in the car for five minutes before I drive home, just to let the day go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: good, now can we talk about the real problem, which is not enough doctors and not enough time. At the union branch meeting I'd probably joke about all the money spent on chatbots that could have paid for two more nurses. Online I mostly keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a relief. I've been dreading the day Martin, our practice manager, makes the AI note-taker compulsory, and in this picture that day either never comes or doesn't matter much. My job is safe, the pay is decent, and Hana and I live rent-free in my grandmother's old flat. The thing that still nags at me is the health centre's contract, which the council puts out to tender again in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep going to the union branch once a month and push for longer appointments for patients with three or more conditions. And I'd keep putting a third of my pay into savings like I do now, because I don't trust that the contract renewal will go smoothly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, and a bit flat. Nothing gets better for my patients just because the robots didn't come. The waiting list for mental health support is still eleven months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the contract. What happens to you if a private company wins it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably be on a new contract with worse terms, or I'd leave, because there are three other practices within twenty minutes that are always advertising. I'd be fine. My worry is the patients, because the last private firm that ran a clinic across town cut the interpreter budget in its first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace if she asked whether to learn the AI tools anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn them if she wants, it's her career. But I'd also tell her that the hours she spends learning software are hours nobody pays her for. I'm stubborn about that, I know.

say: **More doctors** and **more time** matter far more than another chatbot in the clinic.
At the **union branch** I'd joke that chatbot money could have paid for two more nurses.
think: I'm **relieved** the AI note-taker may never become compulsory at the health centre.
My **job and pay** feel safe, and living rent-free in my grandmother's flat helps.
The council's **contract tender** in 2028 still nags at me.
do: **Carry on** working the way I do now, typing my own notes.
Go to the monthly **union meeting** and push for longer slots for complex patients.
Keep saving **a third of my pay** in case the contract renewal goes badly.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, but flat, because patients still wait **eleven months** for mental health support.
S0.quote: Nothing gets better for my patients just because the robots didn't come.
fieldNote: His **relief** is about not being forced onto AI tools, not about money.
His worry points at **patients** and the clinic contract, rarely at himself.
He admits being **stubborn** about unpaid time spent learning software.

steps.text: Keep typing own notes and seeing patients in fifteen-minute slots
Push the union branch for longer slots for complex patients
Put a third of each month's pay into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say what I'd say at a union meeting: if software saves time, that time belongs to patients, not to the budget. I'd be the one at the staff meeting asking who checks the AI's letters when it gets a dose wrong. I'd sign every open letter going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Martin and the council would use it to fill the rota with fewer doctors and more staff on cheaper contracts, with the software doing the thinking. Booking, referral letters and repeat prescriptions are a big chunk of my week, and those are exactly the tasks on that card. I'm good with patients, but I'm slow with new systems, and in a place like ours the slow ones get their sessions cut first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get the union to negotiate a written agreement that no doctor's sessions get cut because of software. I'd go to the training because I'd have to, but I'd keep checking every letter myself, even if it makes me slower. And I'd stop looking at the car I was going to replace and keep that eighteen thousand in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly, and a bit cornered. I'm 27 and I already feel like the old guy who won't use the new printer. That's not a nice thing to find out about yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the health centre do you think would feel it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The receptionists, without a doubt. Dawn on the front desk has been there nineteen years and knows every family on the estate, and an AI phone line would replace half of what she does. Then probably the locums, the stand-in doctors we hire for a day at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep checking everything yourself, but also that slow doctors get cut. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I think I'd end up using it for the dull parts, like booking and letters, and refuse it in the consulting room itself, when I'm actually talking to a patient. I'd lose a session a week, maybe, and I'd live with that before I'd let software into the room with a frightened patient.

I'd ask at staff meetings who **checks the AI** when it gets a dose wrong.
think: Managers would use AI to run the rota with **fewer doctors** on cheaper contracts.

feel: **Tired** and a bit **cornered**, like the old guy who won't use the printer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that health care isn't a product and that a machine can't be held responsible when a patient dies. I'd be on every picket and every panel the union could find. I'd want a law saying a human doctor signs off on every diagnosis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2028 the software would be a better diagnostician than me, and I'd know it. The clinic would need maybe half the doctors, and the ones they kept would be the ones happy to supervise screens. I'm not that doctor. I've got savings and no kids, so I wouldn't go hungry, but I could easily be out of medicine by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd join the union's working group on AI, because if it's coming in two years someone has to fight over the terms now. I'd stop spending on anything big and get our savings up to two years of costs, which is doable with no rent. Once it arrives, I'd take whatever human-only work is left, like home visits and end-of-life care, even if it pays less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I spent nine years training, counting medical school, to be the person who works out what's wrong. If a machine does that better within two years, I don't know what I am at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With robots coming around 2031, what part of your job do you think lasts longest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on bits and the sitting with people. Examining a child's chest, taking a smear, holding someone's hand when I tell them it's cancer. With three years before the robots, home visits to the dying would be the last thing anyone automates, and that's where I'd want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hana that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hana we're okay for money and that I'm not okay in my head. She'd tell me to stop catastrophising and make dinner. Then we'd probably talk about whether she should go back to full-time social work so I could retrain, which is a strange conversation to have at 27.

say: **Health care** isn't a product, and machines can't be **held responsible** for a death.
I'd want a **law** saying a human doctor signs off every diagnosis.
think: By 2028 the software would be a **better diagnostician** than me.
The clinic would need about **half the doctors**, and I'm not the screen-supervising kind.
Savings protect me, but I could be **out of medicine** by thirty.
do: Join the union's **AI working group** now, while the terms are still open.
Build savings to **two years** of costs, helped by paying no rent.
Move into **home visits** and end-of-life care once AGI arrives, even for less pay.
feel: Like the **floor has gone** from under nine years of training.

S2.quote: I spent nine years training, counting medical school, to be the person who works out what's wrong.
fieldNote: Money is not the fear; his **identity** as the doctor who works things out is.
He points to **dying patients** at home as the last human corner.
He's already weighing Hana going **full-time** so he could retrain.

steps.text: Join the union's working group on AI terms this year
Campaign for a law that a human doctor signs every diagnosis
Build savings up to two years of household costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but with more time to organise it properly. I'd say we have five years to write the rules, and if we waste them, that's on the politicians, not on the machines. I'd want a public inquiry before the first clinic swaps a doctor for software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is just long enough to fool myself. I'd be 32, still early in my career, and I can picture myself telling everyone it's fine right up until the letter about restructuring arrives. The thinking part of my job goes in 2031, and the examining goes around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to do a diploma in palliative care, the care of people who are dying, because that's the work I trust least to a machine. I'd keep saving, though less hard than in the two-year picture. And I'd stand for the union's local committee, which I've been avoiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panicked, but the knot's still there. Having five years means I'd have no excuse if I sat on my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra three years change whether you'd retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. With two years I'd only have time to hang on. With five I could actually finish a diploma and change what kind of doctor I am, without changing that I'm a doctor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies selling it and the governments buying it cheap. Not the patients, and not really the doctors who use it either, though I'd struggle not to be angry at the ones who cheered it on.

I'd want a **public inquiry** before any clinic swaps a doctor for software.

Thinking work goes in **2031**, and examining patients follows around **2034**.

Keep **saving**, but less hard than in the two-year picture.
feel: Less panicked, but knotted up, because five years leaves **no excuse** for doing nothing.
S3.quote: Five years is just long enough to fool myself.
fieldNote: He fears his own **complacency** more than the technology itself.
He'd use the time to change **kind of doctor**, not to leave medicine.
He blames **companies** and **governments**, but resents colleagues who cheer AI on.

steps.text: Complete a palliative care diploma within the first two years
Stand for the union's local committee
Keep saving, at a slower rate than in the fast picture

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this decently, if we choose to: retrain people, protect patients, keep a human in charge. I'd probably write something for the union magazine about it, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is long enough that I'd probably do nothing different for the first five, and I know that about myself. The palliative care work would still be my plan, but I'd do it slowly. My worry would shift from me to the receptionists and nurses, who have less cushion than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Canal Street as normal and keep going to the branch. I'd start the palliative diploma around year three instead of now. I'd also put some savings toward Hana and me buying a bigger place, because the flat was always meant to be temporary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not calm. Ten years sounds long until you remember how fast my own training went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 37 in 2036. What would your life look like by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a hospice doctor two days a week and in a clinic the rest, if I'm honest about where I'd end up. Maybe a kid by then. I'd want to be the kind of doctor people ask for when it's serious, not the kind who checks what the screen says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this one that you'd actually welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer forms, if it really takes the paperwork away. And maybe patients wouldn't wait eleven months for therapy if the system had spare capacity. I'd welcome that, I just don't believe the gains would go to the patients by default.

say: **Ten years** is enough to do this decently: **retrain people** and keep humans in charge.
I'd write my first piece for the **union magazine** about it.
think: I'd probably **change nothing** for the first five years, and I know it.
My worry shifts to **receptionists and nurses**, who have less cushion than me.

Put savings toward a **bigger place** with Hana.

S4.quote: Ten years sounds long until you remember how fast my own training went.
fieldNote: He pictures himself as a part-time **hospice doctor** by 37.
He'd welcome **less paperwork** but doubts the gains reach **patients**.
He predicts his own **delay** before I can point it out.

steps.text: Keep working at the Canal Street health centre as normal

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a question. Two years isn't enough for the union, the law or me to catch up, and I'd be the one left holding a stethoscope nobody needs. What would help is a guarantee written into contracts that a human doctor stays responsible for each patient, and paid time to retrain in palliative care.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients who won't use any of it. Half my patients don't have a smartphone that works, and some can't read. If the whole system moves onto apps, those people fall through first, and they're the reason I took this job.

headlineQuote: I'd be the one left holding a stethoscope nobody needs.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old family doctor** at a busy health centre in a poorer district.
He types his own notes, **never uses AI**, and calls himself stubborn about it.
A **union member**, he blames companies and governments, not patients or most colleagues.
His **savings** and rent-free flat protect his money, but not his **sense of purpose**.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, planning a shift toward **palliative care**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for the union, the law or him.
whatWouldHelp: A contract guarantee that a **human doctor** stays responsible for each patient.
**Paid time** to retrain in palliative care.
